content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'hate' in Scripture is most commonly explained not as raw emotional malice but as a Semitic idiom of comparative preference and decisive rejection: to 'hate' something or someone is to love it less, to renounce its claim, or to repudiate allegiance to it in favor of a supreme loyalty (ultimately loyalty to God/Christ). Thus Jesus' demand that disciples 'hate' father, mother, and their own life is read as a call to subordinate every rival attachment to him, and God's 'hatred' (of Esau, of sin, of evildoers' ways) is read as sovereign rejection or covenantal non-election and holy opposition to evil rather than human-style spite.","primary_basis":["Luke 14:26 (whoever does not 'hate' father and mother... cannot be my disciple)","Matthew 10:37 (the parallel showing 'hate' means 'love less than me')","Matthew 6:24 / Luke 16:13 (no one can serve two masters; he will hate the one and love the other)","Genesis 29:30-31 (Leah 'hated' explained by v.30 as 'loved less' than Rachel)","Deuteronomy 21:15-17 (the 'hated' wife = the less-loved wife)","Malachi 1:2-3 and Romans 9:13 ('Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' — read as election/rejection language)","John 12:25 (whoever hates his life in this world will keep it)","Psalm 5:5; Proverbs 6:16-19 (God's hatred of sin and wickedness as holy opposition)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Hate as literal moral evil and the antithesis of Christian love — hatred of a brother is spiritually equivalent to murder and evidence of darkness; this is the plain ethical sense, not an idiom.","basis":["1 John 2:9-11","1 John 3:15","1 John 4:20","Matthew 5:21-22, 43-44 (love your enemies)","Galatians 5:19-21; Titus 3:3"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"Righteous hatred of evil as a positive virtue commanded of believers — to hate what God hates (sin, injustice, false ways) while loving people.","basis":["Psalm 97:10 ('you who love the LORD, hate evil')","Amos 5:15 ('hate evil, love good')","Romans 12:9 ('abhor what is evil')","Psalm 119:104, 128","Proverbs 8:13 ('the fear of the LORD is hatred of evil')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The world's hatred of Christ and his followers as a predicted mark of authentic discipleship and the cosmic conflict between light and darkness.","basis":["John 15:18-25","John 17:14","Matthew 10:22; 24:9","1 John 3:13"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"'Hate' in divine-election texts read as actual divine reprobation/wrath toward persons (a stronger Reformed/double-predestination reading), rather than mere idiom for 'chose the other.'","basis":["Romans 9:13","Malachi 1:2-3","Psalm 5:5; Psalm 11:5"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"'Hate' in Luke 14:26 taken at near-literal force as radical renunciation demanding actual severance from family and self, not merely comparative love (some rigorist, ascetic, or hard-sayings readings).","basis":["Luke 14:26 read without harmonizing to Matthew 10:37","Luke 14:33 (renounce all)"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"Caveat: 'hate' functions more as a recurring lexical/idiomatic term than as a single symbol, so consensus is context-dependent. There is broad, well-settled agreement on two tracks that commentators keep distinct: (1) the Semitic idiom of 'love less / renounce / reject' in discipleship and election passages (Luke 14:26; Gen 29; Rom 9:13), and (2) the plain ethical sense in which interpersonal hatred is condemned as anti-love (1 John). Standard reference works (e.g., major commentaries, TDNT on miseō, lexicons like BDAG) explicitly note the comparative/preferential idiom. If the author's book assigns 'hate' a single unified symbolic meaning beyond these, that would go beyond recognizable consensus."}
